definition: Asymmetry means a lack of balance or matching between two sides or parts — one side differs from the other in size, shape, or share.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word asymmetry. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know asymmetry should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Economists blame the used-car market's troubles on an asymmetry of information: the seller knows the car's history, and the buyer knows the paint.
Unevenness is milder than asymmetry: a surface can be slightly uneven anywhere, while asymmetry indicts the design itself — side measured against side, and failing the comparison.
Lopsidedness is asymmetry grown severe and obvious: nobody needs calipers, because the whole shape visibly heels to one side.
Imbalance means unequal weight or force between two things; asymmetry is the more precise, technical cousin — it points at the mismatch itself, one side measured against the other.
Lopsidedness means leaning visibly to one side; lopsidedness is what asymmetry looks like from across the room — the casual word for a fault grown obvious.

Disparity means a great difference between amounts or levels, usually of resources or outcomes; asymmetry can be tiny — a millimeter's difference is still asymmetry, while disparity implies a gap that matters.

Reviewing the bridge's sensor data, the engineer flagged a slight asymmetry: the east cable was carrying four percent more load than the west, though the design called for a perfect split.
Nothing is broken yet — four percent is small — but the two sides that should mirror each other don't, and that mismatch is what asymmetry names.
Greek a- ('not') joins symmetria ('measuring together'), so the meaning is built right into the word: the sides no longer measure alike.
Asymmetry is the measurer's word for a mismatch — cool, exact, and at home in science and argument alike: asymmetries of information, of power, of load.

No human face is a perfect mirror of itself, and portrait photographers count on that asymmetry.
One eyebrow arches a little higher; one corner of the mouth starts a smile first.
The differences are small -- a few millimeters -- and most people never notice them in the mirror.
But photograph a face, flip the image, and set the two versions side by side: the flipped one looks subtly wrong to everyone who knows the person.
Retouchers who erase every mismatch discover the same thing in reverse.
A perfectly mirrored face stops looking like anyone at all.
